title: English Vocabulary in Use — Advanced (3rd Edition) · Units 09–10
description: Advanced descriptions of people, physique and grooming, facial expressions and gestures, personality traits, sociability, connotation, register and abstract-noun word families.
sourceNotice: Prepared as an independently written personal-study vocabulary package using the user-provided textbook to select targets. Translations, examples and usage notes are original, without reproduction of book passages or exercises.

audit.scope: Teaching and facing exercise pages of Units 9–10 (A–D and A–C), including the illustrated gestures in 9.3 and noun/adjective transformations in 10.3–10.4, checked against the corresponding answer key.
audit.pronunciation: Broad British IPA for high-confidence lexical targets. IPA is deliberately left blank for longer multiword expressions and uncertain noun forms; no full connected-speech transcription is implied.
audit.languagePolicy: All learner-facing fields are in English except Brazilian Portuguese in pt. Vocabulary targets and example sentences are not copied from the source.
audit.reviewMethod: Read teaching pages, exercises and the Unit 9–10 answer keys. Checked lexical meanings, connotations and register; created independent examples and verified word-family exercises, source provenance and TTS targets. Performed static JSON schema and integrity checks. Browser import, TTS output and pronunciation recognition were not tested.
audit.limitations: Includes no MP3 files. Static TTS-target lint does not verify browser pronunciation or sentence-audio behaviour. Physical-description terms such as swarthy, obese and stout should be used sensitively because they may sound dated, medical or intrusive.

units.title: Unit 09 — Describing people: appearance and mannerisms
units.source: English Vocabulary in Use — Advanced (3rd Edition); printed pages 24–25 (PDF pages 26–27).
units.bookTitle: English Vocabulary in Use — Advanced (3rd Edition)
units.category: People and relationships · physical appearance, complexion, expressions and gestures
learningObjectives: Distinguish complimentary, neutral and disapproving descriptions of body shape and weight.
Describe grooming and complexion accurately while recognising potentially loaded or dated descriptors.
Identify facial expressions such as grin, pout, grimace, scowl and leer without confusing their meanings.
Use natural collocations for gestures, mannerisms and nervous habits.

sectionsChecked: A · Adjectives connected with size, weight and general appearance
B · Aspects of appearance and complexion, including embedded glosses
C · Facial expression, including two senses of pout
D · Mannerisms and actions, including paired gestures
Exercises 9.1–9.4, illustrated actions in 9.3, and Unit 9 answer key (PDF pages 216–217)

items.section: A · Size, weight and general appearance
items.example: Her slender figure was accentuated by the long coat.
items.note: Usually complimentary; describes attractive slimness, unlike scrawny.

items.section: A · Size, weight and general appearance
items.example: The rescued puppy looked scrawny after several days without food.
items.note: Disapproving; emphasises unattractive thinness, often with visible bones.

items.pt: alto e desengonçado, com corpo magro
items.section: A · Size, weight and general appearance
items.example: A lanky adolescent struggled to fit into the narrow seat.
items.note: Refers to a tall, thin person whose movements may seem awkward.

items.pt: alto, magro e desengonçado; de membros longos
items.section: A · Size, weight and general appearance
items.example: A gangling young man unfolded himself from the tiny car.
items.note: Particularly common for boys or young men with long, awkward-looking limbs.

items.pt: alto e desengonçado; de braços e pernas compridos
items.section: A · Size, weight and general appearance
items.example: The gangly teenager kept bumping into the low doorway.
items.note: A variant of gangling, with the same ungainly connotation.

items.section: A · Size, weight and general appearance
items.example: The report explored how obesity and poverty can interact.
items.note: A clinical or formal description of very high body fat; it can sound blunt when applied directly to a person.

items.section: A · Size, weight and general appearance
items.example: A stout woman in a navy jacket greeted the visitors.
items.note: Often describes a broad or heavy build; can sound dated, so use tact when describing a person.

items.pt: atarracado; baixo e de tronco largo
items.section: A · Size, weight and general appearance
items.example: The stocky defender was difficult to push off the ball.
items.note: Usually short and broad, particularly across the chest and shoulders; does not necessarily mean overweight.

items.pt: ganhar massa muscular; ficar mais musculoso
items.example: He bulked up during the off-season through strength training.
items.note: In this unit the phrasal verb means increase body size, especially muscle mass.

items.pt: magro e definido; esguio e saudável
items.example: After months of swimming, she felt leaner and stronger.
items.note: Suggests a slim, healthy build; compare scrawny, which is usually negative.

items.example: Despite his size, the wiry climber had remarkable strength.
items.note: A wiry person is thin yet strong, with firm, well-developed muscles.

items.example: The lean and wiry cyclist moved effortlessly up the hill.
items.note: Combines a slender build with physical strength; highlighted in Exercise 9.4.

items.example: His unkempt hair made him look as though he had just woken up.
items.note: Untidy-looking hair or general appearance; kempt is not used as its ordinary positive counterpart.

items.example: She arrived in scruffy jeans and an old jumper.
items.note: Informal, often for untidy or shabby clothing and appearance; a near-synonym given in the unit.

items.example: You should look smart for the reception, even if the event is informal.
items.note: In British English, smart can mean neatly and stylishly dressed, not only intelligent.

items.example: His neat haircut matched his carefully pressed shirt.
items.note: Here it means tidy and carefully arranged, contrasting with unkempt.

items.word: not a hair out of place
items.pt: impecavelmente arrumado; sem um fio de cabelo fora do lugar
items.example: Even after the long ceremony, she hadn't a hair out of place.
items.note: Idiom for a consistently neat, well-groomed appearance; use with have or not have.

items.pt: impecável; sem nenhum defeito ou sujeira
items.example: His shoes were immaculate despite the muddy streets.
items.note: Used of clothes and appearance in flawless, extremely tidy condition.

items.example: The novel describes the sailor as a swarthy, weather-beaten man.
items.note: Traditionally describes a dark complexion; it can sound old-fashioned or loaded, so choose neutral wording when appropriate.

items.pt: tez; aspecto ou tonalidade da pele do rosto
items.example: The harsh light made her complexion look unusually pale.
items.note: The natural colour and appearance of a person's facial skin.

items.pt: de tez amarelada ou pálida com aspecto pouco saudável
items.example: After his illness, his complexion looked rather sallow.
items.note: Describes skin with an unhealthy yellowish or greyish tone; not a general synonym for darker skin.

items.pt: abatido; com aparência cansada e desgastada
items.example: She looked haggard after working through three consecutive nights.
items.note: Suggests visible exhaustion, illness or prolonged strain, especially in the face.

items.pt: sorrir de orelha a orelha; dar um sorriso largo
items.example: He couldn't help grinning when he heard the unexpected news.
items.note: A broad smile, often showing teeth; may express amusement or delight.

items.pt: fazer biquinho com os lábios (para parecer atraente)
items.example: The actor pouted playfully for the publicity photo.
items.note: One sense involves pushing the lips forward deliberately for appearance or a photograph.

items.pt: fazer bico por contrariedade; mostrar desagrado com os lábios
items.example: The child pouted in annoyance when the game ended early.
items.note: Pedagogical phrasing of the second sense taught in the source: pursing the lips to show sulking or displeasure. Both senses use the verb pout.

items.pt: fazer uma careta de dor ou repulsa
items.example: She grimaced at the bitter taste of the medicine.
items.note: Facial expression indicating pain, disgust or embarrassment; do not confuse with a friendly grin.

items.pt: lançar um olhar zangado; franzir a testa com raiva
items.example: The supervisor scowled when another alarm interrupted the meeting.
items.note: A hostile, angry or disapproving facial expression.

items.pt: olhar de maneira lasciva ou insinuante
items.example: The stranger leered at the women, making them uncomfortable.
items.note: A particularly unpleasant gaze, often suggesting unwelcome sexual interest.

items.example: She shrugged her shoulders when asked why the file was missing.
items.note: Often indicates uncertainty, indifference or inability to answer.

items.example: He folded his arms and listened without interrupting.
items.note: A physical posture; may suggest defensiveness in some situations but is not definitive evidence of an attitude.

items.example: She crossed her legs and settled into the armchair.
items.note: A seated posture; distinct from folding your arms.

items.example: His eyelid began to twitch after a stressful afternoon.
items.note: Make small, sudden, usually involuntary movements, often because of nerves or fatigue.

items.example: He bites his nails whenever he is waiting for important results.
items.note: Can be a habitual action or a response to nervousness.

items.pt: cerrar o punho; fechar a mão com força
items.example: She clenched her fist in frustration but chose not to argue.
items.note: Make the hand into a tight fist, frequently associated with anger or tension.

items.example: The boxer clenched his fists before stepping into the ring.
items.note: Plural form used when both hands are closed; also identified in Exercise 9.3.

items.example: He tapped his fingers against the desk while waiting for the reply.
items.note: Usually repeated, light contact on a surface; often conveys impatience.

items.example: She drummed her fingers on the table as the minutes passed.
items.note: A common alternative to tap your fingers, normally suggesting repeated tapping.

units.title: Unit 10 — Describing people: personality and character traits
units.source: English Vocabulary in Use — Advanced (3rd Edition); printed pages 26–27 (PDF pages 28–29).
units.bookTitle: English Vocabulary in Use — Advanced (3rd Edition)
units.category: People and relationships · personality, sociability, character traits and word families
learningObjectives: Distinguish impetuous from impulsive, and self-conscious from conscientious.
Contrast reserved, aloof, haughty, disdainful, diffident and approachable in social contexts.
Use considerate register when describing negative traits such as conceited, pushy and pig-headed.
Form and use abstract nouns such as excitability, gullibility, approachability, impetuosity and obstinacy.

sectionsChecked: A · Adjectives to describe personality or behaviour, including pronunciation of taciturn
B · Sociability, confidence, approachability and attitudes to others
C · Character traits, including naive, gullible, conscientious and obstinate
Exercises 10.1–10.5, the noun–adjective table in 10.3, and the Unit 10 answer key (PDF pages 217–218)

items.pt: impetuoso; precipitado, sem pensar nas consequências
items.example: His impetuous decision to resign left him without a backup plan.
items.note: Typically negative: acting suddenly before considering the consequences.

items.example: An impulsive act of kindness brightened a stranger's day.
items.note: Can be positive or negative; less consistently critical than impetuous.

items.pt: efusivo; muito expansivo ao expressar entusiasmo
items.example: Her effusive praise made the young performers blush.
items.note: For unusually enthusiastic expressions of thanks, welcome or approval, sometimes excessively so.

items.example: The excitable puppy jumped at every unfamiliar sound.
items.note: Easily aroused or excited; not the same as exciting, which describes a thing that causes excitement.

items.pt: insistente de forma inconveniente; ambicioso e intrometido
items.example: The pushy salesperson refused to accept a polite no.
items.note: Informal and disapproving: aggressively promoting personal interests or demands.

items.pt: constrangido; inseguro por se sentir observado
items.example: He felt self-conscious speaking to a room full of experts.
items.note: Feeling awkward because you are aware of others' opinions; contrasts with conscientious.

items.example: She is a well-balanced manager who listens before reaching a decision.
items.note: Describes emotional stability and good judgement.

items.example: The taciturn guide answered only when asked a direct question.
items.note: More formal than quiet; often carries a mildly negative connotation of unwillingness to talk.

items.example: As an introvert, she often recharges by spending time alone.
items.note: Noun for someone oriented towards quiet or solitary activity; not inherently unfriendly or shy.

items.example: His outgoing manner helps him build connections quickly.
items.note: Friendly and confident in company; distinct from the verb go out.

items.example: The extrovert felt energised after hosting a crowded event.
items.note: Person who enjoys social interaction; usually contrasted with introvert.

items.example: The diffident trainee hesitated to ask for clarification.
items.note: Somewhat formal adjective for lacking confidence, especially in social situations.

items.pt: autoestima; avaliação que a pessoa faz de si mesma
items.example: Supportive feedback helped rebuild her self-esteem.
items.note: Often used with high or low; differs from self-importance, an exaggerated sense of status.

items.example: Persistent criticism gradually gave him low self-esteem.
items.note: A frequent collocation meaning a poor opinion of yourself.

items.pt: reservado; pouco expansivo no convívio social
items.example: She seems reserved at first but becomes talkative once she relaxes.
items.note: Not immediately expressive or sociable; does not necessarily indicate hostility.

items.example: His aloof manner was mistaken for arrogance.
items.note: More negative than reserved, suggesting emotional distance or unwillingness to engage.

items.pt: arrogante; altivo; que se julga superior
items.example: She gave a haughty reply to a perfectly reasonable question.
items.note: Disapproving: behaving as though others are beneath you.

items.example: The critic was disdainful of the amateur performance.
items.note: Shows contempt or lack of respect towards something or someone.

items.example: Staff found the director unapproachable during stressful periods.
items.note: People feel uncomfortable starting a conversation with such a person; opposite of approachable.

items.pt: acessível; fácil de abordar; aberto ao diálogo
items.example: An approachable supervisor welcomes questions from new employees.
items.note: Positive quality: easy to speak to and comfortable to ask for assistance.

items.example: He sounded conceited when he claimed nobody else could match his talent.
items.note: Disapproving: having an excessively high opinion of your abilities or attractiveness.

items.pt: presunçoso; que se acha importante demais
items.example: The self-important official demanded special treatment.
items.note: Overstating your own status or importance; contrasted with modest.

items.example: Despite her achievements, she remained remarkably modest.
items.note: Here means not exaggerating your own merits; other senses include small or limited.

items.pt: respeitoso; que trata alguém com consideração
items.example: The debate remained respectful despite strong disagreements.
items.note: Shows consideration, politeness and often admiration; commonly respectful of or towards someone.

items.pt: tratar alguém de igual para igual
items.example: A good mentor treats junior researchers as their equals.
items.note: Means show equal dignity and consideration despite differences in rank or experience.

items.pt: ingênuo; crédulo por falta de experiência
items.example: It would be naive to assume every online review is genuine.
items.note: Can imply lack of experience or unrealistic trust; often less severe than gullible.

items.example: Fraudsters target gullible customers with unrealistic promises.
items.note: Specifically susceptible to being deceived; stronger and more critical than naive.

items.pt: consciencioso; dedicado e cuidadoso nas obrigações
items.example: A conscientious engineer documents every safety-related change.
items.note: Serious and careful about responsibilities; not the same as self-conscious.

items.pt: inquieto; incapaz de ficar satisfeito ou parado
items.example: After several quiet months, he grew restless and looked for a new challenge.
items.note: In this unit, dissatisfied with the current situation and wanting change.

items.example: The obstinate neighbour refused every proposed compromise.
items.note: Usually disapproving: refusing to change views despite reasonable persuasion.

items.example: Stop being so pig-headed and consider the evidence.
items.note: Stronger, more informal and more insulting than obstinate.

items.pt: facilidade de se excitar ou agitar; excitabilidade
items.example: The puppy's excitability made basic training difficult.
items.note: Noun corresponding to excitable; explicitly practised in Exercises 10.3–10.4.

items.example: The scam succeeded by exploiting the victims' gullibility.
items.note: Noun formed from gullible, not gullibleness in standard usage.

items.example: Her disdain for dishonest practices was clear to everyone.
items.note: Noun corresponding to disdainful; also a verb meaning treat with contempt.

items.example: His impetuosity had caused problems in previous negotiations.
items.note: Standard abstract noun corresponding to impetuous; the exercise notes the much rarer impetuousness.

items.example: Her occasional impetuousness surprised her cautious colleagues.
items.note: Much less common noun variant of impetuosity, mentioned in the answer key.

items.example: His obstinacy delayed an agreement for several weeks.
items.note: Noun for the stubborn resistance expressed by obstinate.

items.pt: acessibilidade no convívio; facilidade de se aproximar e conversar
items.example: Her approachability made the new students feel welcome.
items.note: Noun corresponding to approachable; refers to interpersonal ease, not physical accessibility here.

items.example: His natural reserve sometimes came across as disinterest.
items.note: This noun refers to emotional restraint; do not confuse it with a booking or a financial reserve.

items.example: Her initial diffidence disappeared as her confidence grew.
items.note: Noun corresponding to diffident; not the same as indifference.

items.example: The team's progress suffered because of the leader's pig-headedness.
items.note: Informal and disapproving noun derived from pig-headed.

items.example: Mutual respect helped the two groups resolve the dispute.
items.note: Noun paired with respectful; respectful to or towards someone is common.

items.pt: presunção; sentimento exagerado de importância própria
items.example: His sense of self-importance made cooperation difficult.
items.note: Noun corresponding to self-important; usually negative, unlike self-esteem.

items.example: Her modesty impressed the panel as much as her results.
items.note: Noun corresponding to modest in its humility sense.
